newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey to complete Russian gas line study by June.
newsitem.headline: Turkey to complete Russian gas line study by June.

text.p: Turkey's state gas and oil pipeline concern Botas will complete studying by June a proposal from Russian gas monopoly Gazprom to lay a gas pipeline from Russia to Turkey, officials said on Monday.
"Both Botas and Gazprom are carrying out feasibility studies for the pipeline, including for the section under the sea," said a senior Botas official, who declined to be named.
"The results and findings will be completed by the two sides by June, when they will be discussed," she told Reuters.
Gazprom, the world's largest natural gas producer, has entered into a joint venture with the Dutch firm Heerema to oversee the proposal.

According to the Botas official, the proposal envisages building a triple pipeline of about 1,200 km (750-miles) long in total from Izobilnoye, 100 km (63 miles) east of Krasnodar in southern Russia, to the Turkish capital Ankara.
The pipeline will pass about 440 km (275 miles) under the Black Sea from the Russian outlet of Tuapse to Turkey's Samsun port. Its section from Samsun to Ankara will be another 400 km.

"It is not possible to say anything about the feasibility of the project because it will be first of its kind in the world in that it may have to go as deep as some 2,100 metres under sea in some places," the Botas official said.

Officials said the deepest pipeline passage in the world was being carried out at 1,640 metres by a Dutch company for Shell in the Gulf of Mexico. They said underwater pipelines cost about 30 percent more than overland constructions.

Turkey, which annually gets six billion cubic metres (bcm) of gas from Russia, has agreed to tap more gas from its northern neihgbour through the pipeline, which was originally designed to carry up to 16 bcm annually through Georgia and eastern Turkey.

The new accord, which Botas officials say will be finalised soon, will allow Turkey to raise its purchases to a total 30 bcm by the year 2010 by building the eastern line and upgrading the capacity of the existing pipeline through Ukraine, Romania and Bulgaria.
Turkey, in a bid to diversify its natural gas resources, have struck accords with Iran, Algeria, Nigeria, Qatar, Turkmenistan and Yemen to meet its needs of an estimated 40 bcm a year by 2010.
Its 23-year, $23-billion agreement with Iran -- three bcm annually from 1998 later to be raised to 10 bcm from 2005 -- has caused concerns in its chief NATO ally the United States.
Turkey's Islamist-led government has said it will proceed with the gas agreement despite a diplomatic dispute with Iran and opposition from the United States.
Turkey, which desparately needs energy to meet demand that grows at about 12 percent a year, uses 57 percent of its gas imports to produce electricity.
It has begun importing electricity from Iran and Bulgaria.
